Listless means having no energy, no desire, and no interest in doing anything. A listless person feels completely flat — not excited, not motivated, not even curious. They don't want to start anything, finish anything, or engage with anything. It's as if the part of them that normally wants things has gone quiet.

Think of a time you were recovering from a fever. The fever is gone, but you're lying in bed staring at the ceiling. Your phone is right there. Your favourite show is on. There's food in the kitchen. But none of it appeals to you. You don't feel like doing any of it. You're not deeply sad. You're not furious. You're just... empty. Flat. Drained of all "want to."

That hollow, low-energy, nothing-appeals-to-me feeling is exactly what listless describes.
What It Looks Like From the Outside

A listless person tends to move slowly — or barely at all. Their eyes may seem unfocused or distant, like they're looking at something far away even when they're staring at a wall. They speak little, and when they do, their voice is flat. Their posture is slumped. They don't react much to things happening around them — not even things that would normally interest them. They might just sit, or lie down, doing nothing in particular, with no urgency to do anything else.

Listlessness is usually temporary and typically has a clear cause. Common causes include illness or the exhaustion that follows illness, extreme heat, deep disappointment, grief, prolonged boredom, or emotional exhaustion after something stressful or draining. The person isn't choosing to be this way — it's a state that has come over them.

This is where many learners get confused, so pay careful attention to what listless is not.

Listless is not the same as lazy. Laziness is about unwillingness to work — a kind of deliberate avoidance. It's often considered a character habit. Listlessness, on the other hand, is a temporary state that happens to someone. A naturally energetic, hardworking person can become listless. You would never say someone is "being listless on purpose."

Listless is not the same as tired. Tiredness is primarily physical — your body needs rest. Listlessness is more mental and emotional. You can be listless after sleeping ten hours. The tiredness in listlessness is a tiredness of spirit, not just of the body.

Listless is not the same as bored. A bored person still wants something — they just can't find anything interesting enough. A listless person doesn't really want anything at all. Boredom has a kind of restless energy to it. Listlessness has no energy whatsoever.

Listless is not the same as sad. Sadness has an emotional ache — something is wrong and it hurts. Listlessness is more like emotional blankness. The person isn't necessarily hurting; they just feel nothing much. That said, sadness and grief can cause listlessness.

Listless is not the same as apathetic. Apathy suggests a stronger, more settled indifference — someone who simply doesn't care. Listlessness is softer and more temporary. It suggests a person who normally would care, but right now, in this moment, they have no energy to.

Listless sits in the middle range of intensity. It's stronger than "a little tired" or "slightly unmotivated," but it's not the absolute depths of despair or paralysis. It describes a noticeable, observable flatness — enough that other people would likely notice something is off about you.

Listless can describe more than just people. It can describe performances, efforts, conversations, economies, and atmospheres. When used this way, it means lacking vigour, dull, or half-hearted. For example, a listless speech is one with no passion or energy behind it. A listless attempt at something is going through the motions without any real drive.

Here are several examples that show the word being used naturally in different contexts:

  • "She spent the whole Sunday lying on the sofa, listless and uninterested in anything."
  • "The scorching heat left the children listless; they sat in the shade without the energy to even argue."
  • "After weeks of working without a break, he felt listless and struggled to care about anything."
  • "The puppy, usually so bouncy, was listless all morning — a sign it wasn't feeling well."
  • "It was a listless performance from the band; they played the notes but felt nothing."
  • "He made a few listless attempts to clean his room, then gave up and went back to bed."

If you ever need to recall this word quickly: listless means drained of all energy, desire, and enthusiasm — a flat, hollow, nothing-excites-me feeling that is temporary, usually caused by something, and not the same as laziness, sadness, or ordinary tiredness.
